title: US Senate Bill Targets India With 100 Percent Tariffs Over Russian Oil Purchases
excerpt: A bipartisan US Senate bill proposes 100% tariffs on goods from top Russian oil buyers, including India.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A bipartisan US Senate bill proposes 100% tariffs on goods from top Russian oil buyers, including India.
  • The bill was revised from an original 500% tariff to gain broader support among lawmakers.
  • India is among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil, alongside China, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan.
  • Exemptions exist for countries with low Russian gas imports, potentially protecting Japan and France.
  • The bill could significantly escalate trade tensions between India and the United States.

US Senate Bill
  • A bipartisan US Senate bill backed by over 60 lawmakers would impose up to 100% tariffs on goods from the top five buyers of Russian crude oil, including India and China.
  • The legislation, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, was reduced from the original proposal of 500% tariffs to win broader support.
  • India is identified as one of the five largest purchasers of Russian crude, alongside China, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan.
  • The bill includes an exemption for countries whose Russian natural gas imports account for less than 15% of Russia's total gas exports.

A sweeping bipartisan sanctions bill introduced in the US Senate could expose India to tariffs of up to 100% on goods exported to the United States — a direct consequence of New Delhi's continued purchases of Russian crude oil.

The legislation, formally introduced on Thursday with the support of more than 60 co-sponsors from both parties, targets the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas. India, China, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan are identified as the five largest purchasers of Russian crude, putting all five in the crosshairs of potential trade retaliation.

What the Bill Proposes

Named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 — a tribute to the late Republican senator who died suddenly last Saturday — the legislation goes well beyond tariffs. It mandates sanctions against Russia's political leadership, financial institutions, energy sector, defense industrial base, and networks involved in sanctions evasion.

But the tariff provision has drawn the most attention. The bill empowers the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on imports from countries identified as the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, or among the top five facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion.

![Senator Lindsey Graham — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7a/U.S._Senator_Lindsey_Graham%2C_Official_Photo%2C_113th_Congress_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg)

"It imposes tariffs that are targeted: narrowly limited to the five major purchasers — up to 100% — with waiver authority that is narrowly tailored and constricted."

— Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT)

The original version of the bill, introduced in April 2025, proposed a blanket 500% tariff — a figure widely seen as politically unrealistic. The revised 100% cap represents a significant concession designed to secure broader congressional support.

Why India Is in the Crosshairs

India has significantly increased its purchases of Russian crude since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Discounted Russian oil has helped India manage its energy import bill, but it has put New Delhi at odds with Western efforts to constrain Russia's war revenues.

India's Commerce Ministry said it is "closely following developments" regarding the bill, according to India Today. The government has previously maintained that its energy purchases are driven by domestic needs and economic pragmatism, not geopolitical alignment.

The bill includes a provision requiring the US Trade Representative to reassess the top five purchaser list every 180 days and adjust tariff rates based on changes in purchasing patterns — creating a mechanism for countries to reduce their exposure by cutting Russian oil imports.

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

Exemptions and Carve-Outs

The legislation includes a notable exemption: countries whose imports of Russian natural gas account for less than 15% of Russia's total gas exports, and which are taking steps to reduce those imports, would be spared from tariffs. Senate aides said this exemption could protect Japan, France, Hungary, and Belgium.

The bill also excludes the purchase of Russian uranium by the US for its own nuclear reactors and medical isotopes, as well as activities under US-Russia cooperation in the nuclear and space sectors.

Concerns About Presidential Power

Some Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that the bill could give President Trump new authority to impose trade measures on India, Japan, and EU countries, according to Reuters. While the bill includes waiver authority for the president to exempt specific countries, critics worry this creates leverage that could be used for unrelated trade negotiations.

Senate aides for the bill's sponsors expressed optimism about passage. "We're pretty confident on its path," one aide told Reuters, noting the bill had 26 co-sponsors at introduction and expected more within hours.

What This Means for India

Potential Impact on India
›100% tariffs could double costs for Indian exports to the US.
›Affected sectors include IT services, pharmaceuticals, and textiles.
›Legislation adds complexity to India-US trade relations.

For Indian exporters and the broader economy, the bill represents a significant potential escalation in trade tensions with the United States. A 100% tariff on Indian goods — if enacted and applied — would effectively double the cost of Indian exports to the US market, affecting sectors from IT services to pharmaceuticals and textiles.

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the bill adds another layer of complexity to the already fraught India-US trade relationship. The legislation's path through Congress remains uncertain, but its bipartisan support and alignment with the White House's stance on Russia make it a serious policy proposal rather than a symbolic gesture.
